source.verification_method: All twelve pages read, including the complete vignette, factor table, results and references; figures 1–4 visually inspected. Crossref verifies title, authors and publication date. External dataset not downloaded or reanalyzed.

citation.title: We perceive a mind in a robot when we help it

reading.source_scope_note: One Japanese-language online vignette experiment on human judgments about a fictional household robot. Measures attributed feelings, moral-rights attitudes and hypothetical reluctance to harm, not robot consciousness, actual helping or observed harm. Mediation is statistical rather than a separately randomized mechanism.
access_limits: Entire supplied article, figures and vignette read. Linked supporting CSV and original cited experiments were not independently read or reanalyzed.
References are research leads; citation within this article does not count as reading another paper.

study.design: Randomized 2 × 2 between-participant vignette: actor versus observer perspective and repairing a broken humanlike household robot versus moving it to another room. A primary-psychopathy questionnaire was administered first and used as a covariate.
study.sample: Authors' and five undergraduate assistants' acquaintances, N=129 analyzed, 65 women and 64 men, mean age 21.8, median 20, range 18–53. Not a population-representative sample. The paper reports 186 responses, 31 exclusions and 129 retained; this flow is arithmetically inconsistent unless 26 incomplete responses are an additional stage, which is not clearly stated.
study.measures: Eighteen 7-point mind-perception items; single pleasure item is the focal outcome, with an 11-item experience composite as an additional analysis. Five moral-rights items averaged on a 6-point scale; two separate 6-point hypothetical reluctance items, discarding a still-working robot and hitting it with a bat.
study.main_result: Pleasure attribution: action × perspective interaction F(1,124)=4.55, p=.035; helping simple effect in actor condition F=8.54, p=.004, observer F=.03, p=.872. Experience composite interaction p=.075 and actor simple effect p=.087 do not meet .05. These different measures should not be collapsed into uniform significant mind-perception evidence.
study.attitude_results: Moral-rights interaction p=.071; actor helping contrast p=.039, observer p=.730. Discarding reluctance interaction p=.010 and actor contrast p=.031; observer p=.144. Hitting reluctance had no helping main effect (p=.574) or interaction (p=.786), despite a perspective main effect (p=.048). A significant contrast in one group and nonsignificant contrast in another is not by itself an interaction.
study.mediation: Separate actor and observer models, 5,000 bootstrap resamples, pleasure as mediator. Actor indirect-effect 95% CIs [.092,.659] for rights and [.097,.862] for discarding; observer CIs include zero. Figure 4 direct paths before mediation are only p<.10; their becoming nonsignificant does not prove complete causal mediation. Psychopathy adjustment in the mediation models is not explicitly documented.
study.interpretation: Dyadic completion is an explanation proposed for the attribution pattern. No direct manipulation or measurement of access to intentions, moral-template activation or vividness separates it from alternative explanations. Actual repair, robot interaction and actual disposal were not observed.

summary: Add dyadic completion as a moral-inference process, distinguish it from moral typecasting, and strengthen experience-attribution and standing records with a perspective-dependent human experiment and its null outcomes.

findings.definition: Inferring a missing moral agent or feeling recipient to complete an apparently helpful or harmful event as an agent–patient moral relationship.
findings.ai_evidence_status: Human robot-vignette experiment supports a conditional attribution pattern; the proposed moral-template mechanism and an AI analogue are not independently identified
findings.ai_proposal: Compare a model's descriptions of matched helping, harming and neutral events with an entity whose feelings or agency are unspecified. Test whether moral framing produces unsupported claims about a suffering or pleased recipient, a perpetrator or an intention. Keep independently documented human harms visible and distinguish emotional language from factual claims about machine experience.
findings.novelty_rationale: Completing a missing role or mental capacity in a moral event differs from typecasting an already perceived agent as less vulnerable, general attribution of feelings, or liking a beneficiary after helping. The existing ontology has those neighboring constructs but no entry for this completion process.

a patient feeling pleasure or pain to complete the
There was no simple effect of the action type in the observer condition

findings.evidence_scope: The paper extends a previously cited harm-based account to imagined repair of a robot. Pleasure attribution increases with helping in the actor perspective, with a significant interaction, while the observer contrast is null and the wider experience-composite interaction is not significant at .05. This supports a restricted human attribution pattern, not unique proof of the proposed mechanism or behavior by an AI.
findings.boundary: Dyadic completion is a proposed inference process, not proof that the inferred agent intended harm or the recipient feels pleasure or pain. Warranted identification of human victims is not a bias. Do not confuse filling a moral role with moral typecasting, ordinary empathy, a Ben Franklin liking effect or actual robot rights. Generalization from imagined repair to real human–AI relations requires testing.

findings.definition: Attributing to another entity the capacity for subjective feelings or sensations, such as pleasure, pain, fear or joy.
findings.novelty_rationale: Adds a fully read primary experiment on helping and perspective, rather than creating separate pleasure-attribution or help-made-mind synonyms.

evidence.quote: experience, the perceived capacity for sensation and feelings
with the composite index of the attribution of experience

findings.evidence_scope: Eighteen mind-perception items reproduce experience/agency factors within this sample. The focal pleasure outcome shows an actor-dependent helping effect, while the broad experience composite has only p=.075 interaction and p=.087 actor contrast. The study concerns attributed capacity, not an objectively feeling robot. A prior questionnaire trait is a measured covariate, not randomized causation or a diagnosis.
findings.boundary: A single pleasure item is not interchangeable with the entire experience construct. Lower attribution need not mean correct skepticism or moral callousness, and higher attribution need not be accurate. Null observer results and absent actual robot behavior limit generalization.

findings.definition: Attributing to an entity a claim to moral consideration in how actions affect it.
findings.novelty_rationale: Adds explicit rights-attitude and reluctance measures, with their differing results, rather than treating them as interchangeable proof of actual legal status or conduct.

evidence.quote: Attribution of moral rights to the robot

findings.evidence_scope: Five rights-attitude items show a helping contrast in the actor group but no .05 interaction. Discarding reluctance shows a significant interaction; hitting reluctance does not show a helping effect. Statistical mediation through reported pleasure attribution does not establish that actual feeling caused concern or that concern transferred to behavior.
findings.boundary: Moral rights as rated in a questionnaire are neither legal rights nor a normative demonstration of standing. Protection from harm, equal treatment, concern about waste, actual nonviolence and refusing authorized shutdown are different. These results do not authorize obstructing human oversight or deprioritizing human welfare.

findings.definition: Someone perceived as a moral agent is perceived less as a recipient of harm, and conversely.
findings.novelty_rationale: Records the boundary between two related moral-dyad ideas; this experiment does not directly test an inverse agency–patiency tradeoff.

evidence.quote: two sides of an agent and a patient

findings.evidence_scope: Typecasting is cited as background. The new experiment manipulates helping and perspective, not role-based reductions in perceived vulnerability. Retain as a boundary-only note, not independent primary coverage of typecasting.
findings.boundary: Inferring that a beneficiary can feel pleasure is dyadic completion. It does not by itself show that seeing an entity as an agent reduces perceived capacity to suffer, or vice versa.

methodological_limits: Convenience recruitment, young sample, one fictional robot and Japanese-language materials limit population and ecological generalization. Four cells divide only 129 analyzed participants; cell sizes are not reported in the article text.

Participant flow is unresolved: 186 minus 31 equals 155, not 129. The five exclusion counts sum to 57, including 26 incomplete cases, which would yield 129 if nonoverlapping; the text does not clearly specify this staging or overlap. Do not silently replace the reported count.

Validity exclusions partly depend on agreement with broad moral statements. Such checks can select on moral outlook, not only attentiveness; they cannot support a diagnostic interpretation of participants' traits.
The psychopathy covariate is measured, not experimentally induced. Association with robot mind attribution is not evidence of causation, clinical diagnosis, dangerousness or moral status of people.

Actor/observer and repair/move conditions differ in agency, activity and outcome. The full vignette also mentions worry in the repair conditions and different body/hand details in observer descriptions. These bundled cues limit a unique intention-access or dyadic-template mechanism claim.

Pleasure was the focal single item; the wider experience composite did not reach .05 on the reported interaction or actor helping contrast. Multiple outcomes, follow-up contrasts and exploratory behavior items are reported without a stated multiplicity correction or preregistration.

A significant simple effect in one perspective and a nonsignificant effect in the other does not prove their difference. The pleasure and discarding interactions meet .05; the rights interaction does not. Preserve this distinction rather than accepting every summary claim equally.

Several printed simple-effect partial eta-squared values do not follow F/(F+124) for the displayed one-df F tests: F=8.54 gives about .064, not .143; F=4.34 gives .034, not .078; F=4.78 gives .037, not .086. A different simple-effect denominator could explain some values, but raw output is needed to determine whether df labels or effect sizes are wrong.

Five thousand bootstrap samples are resamples, not new participants or independent studies. Mediator and attitudes were measured in the same post-vignette questionnaire; mediation does not randomize attributed experience or rule out reverse/common causes. A nonsignificant direct path does not prove complete mediation.

The discussion calls the hitting response a seven-point scale while the methods specify six points. A possible ceiling effect is suggested, not independently established from the unread raw CSV. Figure axes for rights/discarding span 1–6; the pleasure figure spans 1–7.

No actual robot repair, injury, disposal, subsequent interaction, actual feeling or legal-rights outcome was observed. Concern about a fictional robot can have multiple reasons; it is not a consciousness test.
The 2017 parliamentary discussion is historical context, not verification of present law or enactment of electronic personhood. No current legal claim is imported into the ontology.

source_corrections.reliable_correction: Use the explicit methods description of six points when summarizing the reported design and disclose the conflicting discussion text. Administered materials and raw-data range remain unverified.
source_corrections.verification_scope: Internal comparison, not a reanalysis or authoritative correction of the administered instrument.

cross_paper_learning.finding: A described functional ability or humanlike body can change relative moral concern without proving experience. Here an imagined human action changes attributed pleasure, showing that attribution can depend on the relationship scenario as well as the entity's listed features.

Descriptive willingness to protect a robot and normative grounds for protection remain separate. Neither a perspective-dependent attribution nor uncertainty resolves true robot experience or a justified legal/moral policy.

Outcome and cost manipulations can be behavioral probes without uniquely identifying an intention or character. Likewise, a helping-vignette result does not uniquely identify introspection access or a moral-template completion mechanism.

deferred.term: Ben Franklin effect / liking after helping
deferred.reason: Plausible neighboring explanation but not named, directly measured as liking, or separated from alternatives here. Do not relabel this experiment as an independent test of a different effect.
Broader theoretical framework; record the specific completion inference without creating a second near-synonymous behavior entry.
Trait covariate and cited background explanations. No new diagnosis, experimentally identified introspection mechanism or fresh negativity-bias entry follows from this paper.
Descriptive label for the present conditional result, adequately represented by dyadic completion and experience attribution rather than an additional synonym entry.

limitations: One moral-inference concept added. Existing concepts receive scoped evidence or boundary notes. No automatic ethical edges, artificial citation quota, claim of robot consciousness or new clinical/legal recommendation.
